what_it_is: A static benchmark of 1,200 physics problems from college entrance exams (Gaokao, JEE Advanced, Chinese mock exams) and physics olympiads (IPhO, APhO, EPhO): 25% knowledge-based and 75% reasoning-based, split into easy, medium and hard, 81% with diagrams (pp. 1, 3, 13). Every problem carries an annotated step-by-step solution in which each step records the theorem, target, formula and value; solutions average 8.1 steps, 15.6 for hard problems (pp. 1-3, 14-15). The PSAS framework scores answers (PSAS-A) and steps (PSAS-S): an LLM extracts the model's counterpart of each annotated step, scores its formula and value at 0.5 each, locates the first error step and classifies its type (pp. 4-6). 15 models are evaluated; Deepseek-R1 leads with 56.75 at answer level and 73.26 at step level (pp. 6-7).
domain: physics at college-entrance-exam and olympiad level: classical, quantum and fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetics, optics, relativity (pp. 3-4)
size: 1,200 problems (300 knowledge, 300 each easy, medium, hard), covering 147 theorems; a 200-problem PhysReason-mini subset; 15 models evaluated (pp. 1, 3, 6)
source_of_items: exams and competitions: 1,254 PDFs holding over 20,000 problems (Gaokao 2010-2024, JEE Advanced 2010-2024, Chinese mock exams 2015-2024, IPhO 2008-2021 and others), parsed with MinerU, deduplicated, filtered and translated (pp. 3, 13)
has_gold_traces: yes: an annotated step-by-step solution for every problem, with a Step Analysis giving each step's theorem, target, formula and value (pp. 2-3, 14-15)
evaluation: LLM judge at answer level and step level: PSAS-A extracts each sub-question's answer and checks it against the annotation, weighted by annotated solution length; PSAS-S maps model content onto each annotated step, scores formula (0.5) and value (0.5), finds the first error step and assigns one of seven error types (pp. 4-6). The scoring model is Deepseek-V3 (p. 6).
human_validation: 1,000 of 8,400 model solutions were manually annotated for answer correctness and the location of the first error step; on them PSAS reaches 98.96-99.35% answer accuracy and 97.23-98.04% first-error-step accuracy, against 87.81-93.31% and 33.18-37.54% for direct LLM evaluation (Table 2, p. 6). The annotators are four graduate students from engineering disciplines who are co-authors (p. 19); no inter-annotator agreement is reported. Translations were verified by engineering PhD candidates (pp. 3, 14).
contamination_measures: search prevention: problems whose solutions and answers a five-minute Google search finds are excluded, following GPQA (pp. 3, 14); the items are otherwise static and come from public exams

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1: 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2: 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: S-P1's 'test the application of reasoning to natural laws' fits a benchmark built on applying physics theorems (pp. 1, 3). But the May text omits what matters most for EngTrace's comparison: PhysReason pairs every problem with an annotated step-by-step solution and evaluates model solutions step by step, locating the first error, with the step evaluator checked against 1,000 manually annotated solutions (pp. 2-6; Table 2, p. 6). The section's conclusion that 'existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching' (S-E3) and the Introduction's 'no existing benchmark verifies this process' are contradicted by a paper the section itself cites. S-P2's 'theoretical physics' is loose: these are exam and olympiad problems that the authors say test theorems 'under idealized conditions' (p. 9).

suggested_wording: PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) goes further: each of its 1,200 exam and olympiad physics problems carries an annotated step-by-step solution, and an LLM scores each annotated step's formula and value and locates the first error, an evaluator checked against 1,000 manually annotated solutions; its problems, however, are static, and its step judge is itself an LLM.
facts_to_cite: 1,200 problems from college entrance exams and physics olympiads, 25% knowledge-based and 75% reasoning-based in three difficulty tiers; 81% include diagrams (pp. 1, 3).
Each problem has an annotated step-by-step solution, each step with its theorem, target, formula and value; 8.1 steps on average, 15.6 for hard problems (pp. 1-3).
PSAS-S scores model solutions step by step, formula and value at 0.5 each, and locates the first error step (Algorithm 1, p. 5).
On 1,000 manually annotated solutions, PSAS locates the first error step with 97.23-98.04% accuracy, against 33.18-37.54% for direct LLM evaluation (Table 2, p. 6).
Problems whose answers a five-minute Google search finds are excluded (p. 3).
The best model, Deepseek-R1, scores 56.75 at answer level and 73.26 at step level (Table 3, p. 7); answer-level scores fall from 75.11 on knowledge problems to 31.95 on hard ones (p. 1).
The authors say the problems test physics theorems 'under idealized conditions' rather than real-world scenarios (p. 9).
overlap_with_engtrace: The closest physics precedent in this batch. Shares: gold step-level solutions; step-level evaluation with first-error localisation; difficulty tiers defined by solution length; a human check of the step evaluator. Lacks: generated instances (static public exam items, protected only by search prevention); deterministic step checks (extraction, matching and scoring are all done by an LLM, Deepseek-V3, which is also one of the evaluated models); credit for valid alternative paths (steps are matched to one annotated solution, whereas EngTrace's milestones are order-free); engineering domain (physics only); independent expert validation with agreement statistics (the annotators are co-authors, and no agreement is reported).
notes: The scoring model Deepseek-V3 (p. 6) is also among the evaluated models (Table 3, p. 7), as is Gemini-2.0-Flash, the alternative scorer: a self-evaluation the paper does not discuss, relevant to the planned judge-validity paragraph. Section 5.1 says 15 models; Appendix H says 'seventeen' (pp. 6, 18). The May reference list misprints 6 of the 9 first names against p. 1 (e.g. 'Xinyi' for Xinyu Zhang, 'Jielin Liu' for Jun Liu). If the revision keeps the claim that prior benchmarks only match outcomes, it must exempt PhysReason, or the claim is false.
